The rate bound $M_n:=\max_{x\in K_n}\lambda(x)$ is therefore finite. For fixed ordered channel labels $j_1,\ldots,j_m$, the density of event times $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$ before the first exit is the product of the successive channel rates and exponential no-event factors. Summing over channel labels bounds this density by $M_n^m$, since at each event the sum of active channel rates is at most $M_n$. The ordered simplex has volume $T^m/m!$, so the probability of at least $m$ events before exit by $T$ is at most $(M_nT)^m/m!$, which tends to zero. Thus infinitely many jumps cannot occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

Stop the process at $\tau_n:=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t\notin K_n\}$. The stopped path takes values in the finite set $F_n$ and is frozen after exit. Let $C_n=\max_{y\in F_n}V(y)$. Conditional on the reaction history through time $s$, partition on the finite vector of last-used stream indices; on each part [F3] gives independence of all unused coordinates. If $s$ falls within a holding interval, the residual exponential wait has the same law because $e^{-\lambda(w+u)}/e^{-\lambda w}=e^{-\lambda u}$. Thus for $x=X_s\in K_n$, the density of one channel-$j$ event at elapsed time $u$ and no earlier event is $a_j(x)e^{-\lambda(x)u}$. The probability of at least two events within $h$ is at most $(M_nh)^2/2$ by integrating the summed first-two-event density, bounded by $M_n^2$, over the ordered two-time simplex. Since $V\le C_n$ on $F_n$, the first-event term differs from $h(QV)(x)$ by at most $C_nM_n^2h^2/2$, using $|1-e^{-z}|\le z$ for $z\ge0$; the multiple-event remainder is bounded by $2C_n(M_nh)^2/2$. Thus, uniformly over $x\in K_n$, $\mathbb E[V(X_{(s+h)\wedge\tau_n})-V(X_{s\wedge\tau_n})\mid\mathcal F_s]=h\,1_{\{s<\tau_n\}}(QV)(X_s)+O(h^2).$ Summing this identity on a uniform partition of $[0,t]$ and letting the mesh tend to zero gives $\mathbb E[V(X_{t\wedge\tau_n})]=V(x_0)+\mathbb E\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}(QV)(X_s)\,ds.$ The error sum is $O(th)$; the Riemann sums converge because the stopped path has finitely many jumps by step 1.1 and $QV$ is bounded on $K_n$.
